opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, world models aren't a side branch of AI; they're close to the core question of what intelligence actually is.

Over the last few years, large language models have shown how far you can get by learning from text, and that progress is real. But language is a very compressed, very human-filtered description of the world. It's what we chose to write down. A lot of what makes an animal, or a child, intelligent happens before language: understanding that objects persist when you look away, that things fall, that if you push something it moves, that space has structure. That kind of knowledge is mostly not in text, or only shows up indirectly.

So a world model, to me, is a system that builds an internal representation of how the world works, so it can predict, imagine, and plan, rather than just produce plausible outputs. The key isn't generating pretty videos. Video generation is one way to probe it, but a model can generate convincing pixels without understanding physics or causality. What we want is a model whose internal state captures the right abstractions, so you can ask "what happens if I do this?" and get a meaningful answer.

I think of the broader trajectory in a few layers. First, we learned to model language well. The next frontier is grounding: connecting those systems to perception, especially vision, and to space and time. After that comes action: agents that use their world model to make decisions in the physical world, which is where robotics and embodied AI come in. Without a good world model, it's hard to see how you get reliable embodied intelligence, because you can't learn everything by trial and error in the real world. You need to simulate in your head.

There's also a methodological point I care about. Much of the field has assumed that if you scale up language and bolt vision on as an adapter, you'll get there. I'm not fully convinced. Visual representation learning, spatial reasoning, and multimodal understanding probably need to be first-class citizens, not afterthoughts. When we test today's multimodal models on fairly simple spatial reasoning, like counting objects, judging relative distance, or remembering the layout of a room from a video, they often fail in ways a young child wouldn't. That tells me something is missing in the foundations.

So I see world models as the bridge from today's AI, which is very good at manipulating symbols, to an AI that understands and acts in the world we live in. It's still early. We don't yet agree on the right objective, the right architecture, or even the right benchmarks. But that's what makes it exciting. It feels a bit like the early days of deep learning in vision, when the big questions were still open.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression from language modeling to grounding and action, but does not characterize it as a progression from representation learning and supervised learning.

r002.rationale: It does not say that “world model” is a catch-all label researchers apply too broadly.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that using “world model” as a buzzword could help the field advance.

r004.rationale: It contrasts world models with language models, but does not endorse the specific “world model” versus “word model” distinction.

r005.rationale: It calls world models a bridge toward AI that understands and acts in the world, but does not present them as a shared eventual destination for AI research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "world model" has become one of those terms where everyone agrees it matters and nobody quite agrees on what it means. So let me try to say what I mean by it.

For a long time, the dominant story in AI has been language. Language models got scaled up, they got surprisingly capable, and a lot of people started to believe that language was the substrate, that if you just kept going, everything else, vision, reasoning, acting in the world, would fall out as a byproduct. I never fully bought that. Language is a compressed, lossy record of human experience. It's incredibly useful because humans already did the hard work of abstracting the world into symbols. But the world itself is not made of tokens. It's continuous, it's spatial, it has physics, it has objects that persist when you're not looking at them. A child learns most of that before they can say a single sentence.

So when I think about world models, I think of them as the attempt to learn that other half directly. Not "describe what's in this image," but "understand what will happen next, what's behind that object, what happens if I push this." A representation of the world that supports prediction and planning and interaction, not just description.

And I'd frame it as the next real frontier for a few reasons. First, the data is different. The internet text is largely exhausted, in the sense that we've basically scraped it. But video, sensor data, embodied experience, that's effectively unbounded, and it hasn't been mined in anything like the same way. Second, the capability it unlocks is different. If you want robots, if you want agents that act in physical or even complex digital environments, they need to anticipate consequences. You can't do that purely by pattern-matching over text. Third, and this is the part I care most about as a researcher, I think it forces us to revisit some foundational questions about representation learning that the language boom let us skip over. What does a good visual representation actually look like? How much of understanding is in the predictive structure versus the generative detail? Those were questions in self-supervised learning five or six years ago, and they're coming back with much higher stakes.

Now, I want to be a bit careful here, because there's a lot of hype. People see a video generation model producing something that looks physically plausible and say, "Look, it learned physics." I'm more skeptical. Looking right and being right are not the same thing. A model can generate a very convincing ball bouncing and still have no usable internal notion of gravity that you could plan with. So one of the things I think the field has to get much more serious about is evaluation. We need to ask whether these models actually have a world, or whether they've just gotten very good at rendering one.

My own view is that the generative route and the representation route are going to converge. The visual generation models are, in a sense, forced to learn a lot about the world to produce coherent output, and the representation-focused work gives you the handle to actually use what was learned. The interesting research is at that intersection. And the relationship to language is not a competition. The end state is a system that has grounded perception of the world, can reason about it, and can talk about it. Language models gave us the last two in a sort of hollow form. World models are how you fill in the ground underneath.

So in the broader arc, I'd say we've just finished the chapter where AI learned to read what humans wrote. The next chapter is where it learns to look at the world for itself. That's going to be slower, messier, and much more dependent on actual research rather than just scaling, and personally I think that's exactly why it's worth working on.

r002.rationale: It says people disagree about what “world model” means, but does not say researchers apply the label too broadly to their work.

r005.rationale: It calls world models a frontier and describes an integrated AI system as an end state, but does not present world models as a shared eventual destination for AI research.

astra-6.text:
I think world models get at a fundamental question: what does an AI system need to understand in order to act in the world? Recognizing an object or generating a plausible image is useful, but you also want a system to anticipate what happens next. If I take an action, how will the situation change? What can I control, and what am I uncertain about?

That connects perception, prediction, and action. For example, a robot reaching for a cup needs more than the label “cup.” It needs some understanding of space, motion, and the consequences of contact. A world model could help it reason about those consequences before acting.

Video is an interesting direction because it contains observations of how the world changes. But predicting what looks plausible isn’t necessarily the same as understanding what will happen when you intervene. That distinction matters, especially if we want these systems to support planning.

So I see world models as an important part of the broader development of AI, alongside language and reasoning. The real test is whether learning a model of the world helps a system make better decisions, adapt to unfamiliar situations, and learn from its mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models get at a fundamental question: what does it mean for an AI system to understand the world? A model can recognize objects or generate a convincing video, but can it predict what happens when something changes—especially when it takes an action?

For me, the interesting direction is learning representations that capture those dynamics. If I push an object, how will it move? If I take a different action, what outcome should I expect? That connects perception with prediction, planning, and eventually interaction.

I wouldn’t treat world models and language models as competing paths. Language gives us an incredibly rich description of human knowledge. But there’s also knowledge we acquire through seeing and interacting that’s difficult to express in words. The broader opportunity is to bring those capabilities together.

The challenge is figuring out what a model actually needs to predict. Predicting every pixel may not be necessary for making a good decision. A useful world model should capture the things that matter for the task, and we should evaluate it through what it enables a system to do.
